title: Electrochemistry
overview: Use standard electrode potentials to calculate cell potentials and predict whether a redox reaction is feasible. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Define standard electrode potential and use the standard hydrogen electrode.
Write cell notation and calculate E°cell.
Predict the feasible redox direction and discuss limitations of E° predictions.
Use Q=It and F to calculate quantities in electrolysis.

definitions.definition: The emf of a half-cell relative to the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions, written as a reduction.
The reference half-cell with E°=0.00 V.
An ionic connection that completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality without bulk mixing.
The potential difference between two half-cells.
The charge carried by 1 mol of electrons, approximately 9.65×10⁴ C mol⁻¹.
Using electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous redox process.

sections.title: Half-cells and standard conditions
content: Standard E° values refer to 298 K, solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³ and gases at 100 kPa, measured against the hydrogen electrode. Tables show reduction half-equations; a more positive E° means a greater tendency to be reduced.
bullets: An inert Pt electrode is needed when no conducting solid redox species is present.
Electrons travel through the wire; ions move through the salt bridge.

sections.title: Cell notation and E°cell
content: Write the oxidation half-cell on the left and reduction half-cell on the right, with phase boundaries | and a salt bridge ||. Calculate E°cell=E°right−E°left using reduction potentials. Balance electrons only for the overall equation; never multiply E° values by stoichiometric coefficients.
bullets: The cathode is reduction and the anode is oxidation.

sections.title: Feasibility and limitations
content: A positive E°cell predicts a thermodynamically feasible forward reaction under standard conditions. Actual behaviour can differ because concentrations, gas pressures and temperature are non-standard, reactions are kinetically slow, or activation energy is high.
bullets: Choose the oxidising agent from the more positive reduction potential.
Do not use E° alone to predict rate.

sections.title: Quantitative electrolysis
content: Charge Q=It. Moles of electrons equal Q/F; use the balanced electrode half-equation to convert electron moles to product moles, then to mass or gas volume. Current in amperes is coulombs per second.
bullets: Use the electron coefficient from the half-equation, not the overall equation blindly.

examTips: Write both half-equations before selecting the direction and calculating E°cell.
State standard-condition and kinetic limitations when evaluating a prediction.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Adding two reduction potentials without reversing the oxidation direction conceptually.
Multiplying E° by the electron coefficient.
Using time in minutes in Q=It.

quickRecall.question: Which half-cell is on the right in standard cell notation?
Why are E° values not multiplied when a half-equation is scaled?
quickRecall.answer: Potential is an intensive quantity; scaling amount does not scale voltage.

quickRecall.question: What does positive E°cell predict?
quickRecall.answer: Thermodynamic feasibility of the written cell reaction under standard conditions.

quickRecall.question: How are moles of electrons found from current and time?
quickRecall.answer: Calculate Q=It, then divide by F.
